newsitem.title: USA: Dow nears 6,000, S&P 500 tops 700 after jobs report.
newsitem.headline: Dow nears 6,000, S&P 500 tops 700 after jobs report.

text.p: The Dow industrials surged toward the 6,000 milestone and the S&P 500 topped 700 for the first time as a shockingly weak September payrolls report soothed inflation fears and sparked ferocious bond buying.

"We're nearing my 1996 target of 6,100 and I think the stock market is headed higher than that. This remarkable rise is going to continue well into 1997 at least," said William LeFevre, a senior market analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum.

The Dow Jones industrial average rallied 60.01 points, or 1.01 percent, to a record closing high of 5,992.86 after hitting 5,995.47 earlier. That topped Wednesday's record close of 5,933.97. For the week, the blue chip index was up 119.94 points, or 2 percent.
In the broader market, advancing issues outpaced declines by 1,781 to 694 on very heavy volume of 467 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks cruised through the 700 barrier, surging 8.68 points, or 1.25 percent, to 701.46 and topping Wednesday's record of 694.01. The index has scored record closes four times this week, ending up 15.27 from last Friday.
Likewise, the NYSE Composite index, which scored a record every day this week except Thursday, rose 4.02 to 374.16, an all-time high finish. The index was up 7.89 on the week.
The technology-studded Nasdaq Composite index soared 14.47 points, or 1.17 percent, to 1,247.56, just shy of June 5's record 1,249.15. The index was up 17.51 on the week.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond soared more than a full point, knocking its yield down to 6.75 percent from 6.84 percent at Thursday's close.
Stocks and bonds surged after the government said September non-farm payrolls fell 40,000, sharply weaker than the rise of 166,000 forecast by private economists and August's 241,000 increase.

While analysts deemed the report "one-way good news for bonds," it could prove to be a double-edged sword for stocks if moderating economic growth restrains corporate profit growth, said David Shulman, Salomon's chief equity strategist. "It raises questions for fourth-quarter earnings."

Shulman said investors were "coming to grips with a single-digit earnings growth environment," seeking out the technology, defensive and interest-rate sensitive issues that might outperform the broader market.

Several analysts expressed concern that a weaker economy would erode corporate profits in this sixth year of the bull market, the most powerful in history. But LeFevre, who started working on the Street when the Dow was at 160, was optimistic.

"Every bull market has a wall of worry and there are a lot of worrywarts out there," he said. "Today's mutual fund investors are investing for new homes, college and retirement -- none of which will be reached in the next week or next month or next year. They view dips as a buying opportunity."

Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management, said the employment report was sufficiently weak to "severely lessen the chance that the Fed will raise short-term interest rates at its Nov. 13 FOMC meeting."

The Dow's ascent was aided by components Du Pont, up 3 to 93-3/8, GE, up 1-3/4 to 93-5/8, International Business Machines Corp., up 1-7/8 to 126-7/8, Procter & Gamble, up 1-3/4 to 99-7/8, and Exxon Corp., up 1-3/4 to 87-7/8.
Among special situations, Dow component Alcoa slipped 3/8 to 60 after hitting a low of 57-1/8 after it reported lower-than-expected third quarter earnings.
Stratus Computer surged 3-3/8 to 23-1/8. Salomon Brothers upgraded Stratus to strong buy from buy on the stock's "compelling" share price.

Those warning of earnings disappointments included Parker Hannifin, down 3-7/8 to 38-1/8, Raytheon off 4-1/8 to 49-7/8, Dole Food down 2-7/8 to 40-1/8. Redhook Ale fell 4-1/16 to 17, Gensym tumbled 8-1/2 to 12-1/2, LSI Industries lost 3-5/8 to 12-1/8 and SS&C Technologies shed 3-5/8 to 6-1/8.
The American Stock Exchange index rose 7.29 to 579.89, up 11.42 on the week.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 6,885.591, up 74.097, or 1.09 percent. It was up 131.262 on the week.
